rows.stem: If \(7\cos^2\theta + 3\sin^2\theta = 4\), then the value of \(\theta\) is :
rows.solution:
Write \(7\cos^2\theta + 3\sin^2\theta = 3(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta) + 4\cos^2\theta = 3 + 4\cos^2\theta\).

So \(3 + 4\cos^2\theta = 4\), giving \(\cos^2\theta = \dfrac{1}{4}\) and \(\cos\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}\) (for an acute angle). So \(\theta = 60^\circ\), which is option (C) \(60^\circ\).

rows.subtopic: Probability from a Collection of Objects
rows.stem: The probability of drawing an even prime number out of numbers from 1 to 30 is :
rows.solution:
The only even prime is 2, so exactly 1 of the 30 numbers is favourable.

\(P(\text{even prime}) = \dfrac{1}{30}\), which is option (A) \(\dfrac{1}{30}\).

rows.stem: The quadratic equation whose roots are 7 and \(\dfrac{1}{7}\) is :
rows.solution:
The sum of the roots is \(7 + \dfrac{1}{7} = \dfrac{50}{7}\) and the product is \(7 \times \dfrac{1}{7} = 1\).

A quadratic with these roots is \(x^2 - \dfrac{50}{7}x + 1 = 0\), that is \(7x^2 - 50x + 7 = 0\), which is option (A) \(7x^2 - 50x + 7 = 0\).

rows.subtopic: HCF and LCM by Prime Factorisation
rows.stem: The least number which is a perfect square and is divisible by each of 16, 20 and 50, is :
rows.solution:
A number divisible by each of 16, 20 and 50 is a multiple of their LCM.

\(16 = 2^4\), \(20 = 2^2 \times 5\), \(50 = 2 \times 5^2\), so LCM \(= 2^4 \times 5^2 = 400\).

Every exponent in \(400 = 2^4 \times 5^2\) is even, so 400 is already a perfect square (\(20^2\)). The least number that is a perfect square and divisible by all three is therefore 400.

400 is not among the printed choices (3600 is a perfect square divisible by all three, but it is not the least). The marking scheme acknowledges this: no option is correct, and full marks are awarded for every attempt.

rows.stem: The coordinates of the end points of a diameter of a circle are \((5, -2)\) and \((5, 2)\). The length of the radius of the circle is :
rows.solution:
The diameter joins \((5, -2)\) and \((5, 2)\), so its length is \(\sqrt{(5 - 5)^2 + (2 + 2)^2} = 4\).

The radius is half of this, 2 units (a length is never negative, so \(\pm 2\) is not a radius). This is option (D) 2.

rows.stem: The points \((-5, 0)\), \((5, 0)\) and \((0, 4)\) are the vertices of a triangle which is a/an :
rows.solution:
Let the points be \(P(-5, 0)\), \(Q(5, 0)\) and \(R(0, 4)\).

\(PQ = 10\), \(PR = \sqrt{25 + 16} = \sqrt{41}\), \(QR = \sqrt{25 + 16} = \sqrt{41}\).

Two sides are equal and \(PR^2 + QR^2 = 82 \neq 100 = PQ^2\), so it is isosceles and not right-angled. This is option (B) isosceles triangle.

rows.stem: In the given figure, RS is the tangent to the circle at the point L and MN is the diameter. If \(\angle NML = 30^\circ\), then \(\angle RLM\) is :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - which side of L the point R lies on (towards M) is fixed only by the drawing, and it decides between the two angles the tangent makes with LM. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
MN is a diameter, so \(\angle MLN = 90^\circ\) (angle in a semicircle). In triangle MLN, \(\angle MNL = 180^\circ - 90^\circ - 30^\circ = 60^\circ\).

The angle between the tangent and the chord LM equals the angle in the alternate segment: \(\angle RLM = \angle LNM = 60^\circ\).

(Or: the radius OL is perpendicular to RS, and \(\angle OLM = \angle OML = 30^\circ\) since \(OL = OM\), so \(\angle RLM = 90^\circ - 30^\circ = 60^\circ\).) This is option (B) \(60^\circ\).

rows.stem: In the given figure, \(PQ \parallel BC\). If \(\dfrac{AP}{PB} = \dfrac{4}{13}\) and AC = \(20{\cdot}4\) cm, then the length of AQ is :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - that P lies on AB and Q on AC is shown only in the drawing. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
\(PQ \parallel BC\), so by the Basic Proportionality Theorem \(\dfrac{AQ}{QC} = \dfrac{AP}{PB} = \dfrac{4}{13}\).

So \(\dfrac{AQ}{AC} = \dfrac{4}{4 + 13} = \dfrac{4}{17}\), and \(AQ = \dfrac{4}{17} \times 20{\cdot}4 = 4{\cdot}8\) cm. This is option (D) \(4{\cdot}8\) cm.

rows.stem: Which of the following statements is *incorrect* ?

options.label: A
options.text: Two congruent figures are always similar.

options.label: B
options.text: A square and a rhombus of the same area are always similar.

options.label: C
options.text: Two equilateral triangles are always similar.

options.label: D
options.text: Two similar triangles need not be congruent.

rows.solution:
Congruent figures are similar, all equilateral triangles are similar, and similar triangles need not be congruent: those three statements are true.

A square and a rhombus of the same area are not always similar, because a rhombus need not have right angles while every angle of a square is \(90^\circ\). The incorrect statement is option (B) A square and a rhombus of the same area are always similar.

rows.stem: The sum of the exponents of prime factors in the prime factorisation of 4004 is :
rows.solution:
\(4004 = 2^2 \times 7 \times 11 \times 13\).

The sum of the exponents is \(2 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 5\), which is option (A) 5.

rows.stem: In a cricket match, a batsman hits the boundary 7 times out of the 42 balls he plays. The probability of his *not* hitting a boundary is :
rows.solution:
He does not hit a boundary on \(42 - 7 = 35\) balls.

\(P(\text{not a boundary}) = \dfrac{35}{42} = \dfrac{5}{6}\), which is option (C) \(\dfrac{5}{6}\).

rows.stem: If a large circular pizza is divided into 5 equal sectors, then the central angle of each sector will be :
rows.solution: Five equal sectors share the full angle of \(360^\circ\), so each central angle is \(\dfrac{360^\circ}{5} = 72^\circ\). This is option (D) \(72^\circ\).

rows.stem: If \(\sin 30^\circ \tan 45^\circ = \dfrac{\sec 60^\circ}{k}\), then the value of k is :
rows.solution:
\(\sin 30^\circ \tan 45^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 1 = \dfrac{1}{2}\), and \(\sec 60^\circ = 2\).

So \(\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{2}{k}\), giving \(k = 4\). This is option (A) 4.

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.subtopic: Graphical Method and Nature of Solutions
rows.stem: The line represented by the equation \(x - y = 0\) is :
rows.solution:
\(x - y = 0\) is the line \(y = x\). The point \((0, 0)\) satisfies it, so the line passes through the origin. (It is not parallel to either axis, and \(3 - 2 \neq 0\), so \((3, 2)\) is not on it.)

This is option (C) passing through the origin.

rows.stem: The \(10^{\text{th}}\) term of the AP \(5, \dfrac{19}{4}, \dfrac{9}{2}, \dfrac{17}{4}, \ldots\) is :
rows.solution:
The first term is \(a = 5\) and the common difference is \(d = \dfrac{19}{4} - 5 = -\dfrac{1}{4}\).

\(a_{10} = a + 9d = 5 - \dfrac{9}{4} = \dfrac{11}{4}\), which is option (A) \(\dfrac{11}{4}\).

rows.subtopic: Zeroes and Coefficients of a Quadratic Polynomial
rows.stem: If \(-4\) is a zero of the polynomial \(p(x) = x^2 - x - (2 + 2k)\), then the value of k is :

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.subtopic: Graphical Method and Nature of Solutions
rows.stem: The equation of a line parallel to the x-axis and at a distance of 3 units below x-axis is :
rows.solution: A line parallel to the x-axis has the form \(y = c\). Three units below the x-axis means \(c = -3\), so the line is \(y = -3\). This is option (C) \(y = -3\).

rows.subtopic: HCF and LCM by Prime Factorisation
rows.stem: The HCF of 40, 110 and 360 is :
rows.solution:
\(40 = 2^3 \times 5\), \(110 = 2 \times 5 \times 11\), \(360 = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5\).

The common prime factors, to their lowest powers, are \(2 \times 5 = 10\). The HCF is 10, which is option (D) 10.

rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** Common difference of the AP : \(5, 1, -3, -7, \ldots\) is 4.

**Reason (R) :** Common difference of the AP : \(a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots, a_n\) is obtained by \(d = a_n - a_{n-1}\).
rows.context: Questions number 19 and 20 are Assertion and Reason based questions. Two statements are given, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
In \(5, 1, -3, -7, \ldots\) each term is 4 less than the one before, so the common difference is \(-4\), not 4. The Assertion is false.

The common difference of any AP is a term minus the term before it, \(d = a_n - a_{n-1}\), so the Reason is true.

So the Assertion is false while the Reason is true, which is option (D) Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.subtopic: Consistency from the Ratios of Coefficients
rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** The pair of linear equations \(px + 3y + 59 = 0\) and \(2x + 6y + 118 = 0\) will have infinitely many solutions if \(p = 1\).

**Reason (R) :** If the pair of linear equations \(px + 3y + 19 = 0\) and \(2x + 6y + 157 = 0\) has a unique solution, then \(p \neq 1\).
rows.context: Questions number 19 and 20 are Assertion and Reason based questions. Two statements are given, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
For \(p = 1\): \(\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{3}{6} = \dfrac{59}{118}\), all equal to \(\dfrac{1}{2}\), so the two equations have infinitely many solutions. The Assertion is true.

For the second pair, a unique solution needs \(\dfrac{p}{2} \neq \dfrac{3}{6}\), that is \(p \neq 1\). The Reason is true.

But the Reason is about a different pair of equations and a different condition (unique solutions), so it does not explain the Assertion. This is option (B) Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

rows.subtopic: Zeroes and Coefficients of a Quadratic Polynomial
rows.stem: If p and q are zeroes of the polynomial \(p(y) = 21y^2 - y - 2\), then find the value of \((1 - p) \cdot (1 - q)\).
In the given figure, the shape of the top of a table is that of a sector of a circle with centre O and \(\angle AOB = 90^\circ\). If AO = OB = 42 cm, then find the perimeter of the top of the table.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the drawing shows the table top is the MAJOR sector (the 270 degree part); the words alone do not say which sector. Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
The table top is the major sector: its angle is the reflex angle \(360^\circ - 90^\circ = 270^\circ\).

Perimeter = length of the major arc + 2 radii

\(= \dfrac{270}{360} \times 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 42 + 2 \times 42 = 198 + 84 = 282\) cm.

rows.stem: In the given figure, three sectors of a circle of radius 5 cm, making angles \(35^\circ\), \(50^\circ\) and \(95^\circ\) at the centre are shaded. Find the area of the shaded region. [Use \(\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}\)]
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - three shaded sectors of 95, 50 and 35 degrees; every value is in the stem. Page idx 14.
rows.solution:
The three shaded sectors together have angle \(35^\circ + 50^\circ + 95^\circ = 180^\circ\), so they make up half the circle.

Shaded area \(= \dfrac{180}{360} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 5^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{550}{7} = \dfrac{275}{7} \approx 39{\cdot}29\ \text{cm}^2\).

rows.stem: If \(\tan A = \sqrt{3}\); where A is an acute angle, then find the value of \(\dfrac{\sin^2 A}{1 + \cos^2 A}\).
rows.solution:
\(\tan A = \sqrt{3}\) with A acute, so \(A = 60^\circ\).

\(\dfrac{\sin^2 60^\circ}{1 + \cos^2 60^\circ} = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^2}{1 + \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2} = \dfrac{3/4}{5/4} = \dfrac{3}{5}\).

rows.stem: In the given figure, D is a point on the side BC of \(\Delta ABC\) such that \(\angle ADC = \angle BAC\). Show that \(CA^2 = CD \cdot CB\).
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - triangle ABC with D on BC and the equal angles marked; the stem states the configuration. Page idx 14.
rows.solution:
In triangles ACD and BCA:

\(\angle ADC = \angle BAC\) (given), and \(\angle ACD = \angle BCA\) (the same angle C).

So by the AA criterion, \(\Delta ACD \sim \Delta BCA\).

Corresponding sides are proportional: \(\dfrac{CA}{CB} = \dfrac{CD}{CA}\). Cross-multiplying gives \(CA^2 = CD \cdot CB\).

rows.stem: In the given figure, \(OA \cdot OB = OC \cdot OD\). Show that \(\angle A = \angle C\) and \(\angle B = \angle D\).
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - that AB and CD are straight lines crossing at O (A-O-B and C-O-D) is shown only in the drawing. Page idx 14.
rows.solution:
From \(OA \cdot OB = OC \cdot OD\) we get \(\dfrac{OA}{OC} = \dfrac{OD}{OB}\).

In triangles AOD and COB, \(\angle AOD = \angle COB\) (vertically opposite angles), and the sides including these angles are proportional.

So by the SAS similarity criterion, \(\Delta AOD \sim \Delta COB\), and their corresponding angles are equal: \(\angle A = \angle C\) and \(\angle D = \angle B\).

rows.stem: At point A on the diameter AB of a circle of radius 10 cm, tangent XAY is drawn to the circle. Find the length of the chord CD parallel to XY at a distance of 16 cm from A.
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the circle with diameter AB, tangent XAY at A, and chord CD meeting AB at P; the stem states every value. Page idx 16.
rows.solution:
The diameter AB is perpendicular to the tangent XY at A. Since \(CD \parallel XY\), CD is also perpendicular to AB; let it meet AB at P.

\(AP = 16\) cm and \(OA = 10\) cm, so \(OP = 16 - 10 = 6\) cm.

In right triangle OPC, \(OC = 10\) cm (radius), so \(CP = \sqrt{10^2 - 6^2} = \sqrt{64} = 8\) cm.

A perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, so \(CD = 2 \times CP = 16\) cm.

rows.stem: Prove that : \(\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{\tan^2\theta}\right)\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{\cot^2\theta}\right) = \dfrac{1}{\sin^2\theta - \sin^4\theta}\)
rows.solution:
\(1 + \dfrac{1}{\tan^2\theta} = 1 + \cot^2\theta = \operatorname{cosec}^2\theta\) and \(1 + \dfrac{1}{\cot^2\theta} = 1 + \tan^2\theta = \sec^2\theta\).

\(\text{LHS} = \operatorname{cosec}^2\theta \sec^2\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sin^2\theta} \cdot \dfrac{1}{\cos^2\theta} = \dfrac{1}{\sin^2\theta(1 - \sin^2\theta)} = \dfrac{1}{\sin^2\theta - \sin^4\theta} = \text{RHS}\).

rows.stem: Prove that : \(\sqrt{\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec}\theta - 1}{\operatorname{cosec}\theta + 1}} + \sqrt{\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec}\theta + 1}{\operatorname{cosec}\theta - 1}} = 2\sec\theta\)
rows.solution:
Add the two square roots over the common denominator \(\sqrt{(\operatorname{cosec}\theta + 1)(\operatorname{cosec}\theta - 1)}\):

\(\text{LHS} = \dfrac{(\operatorname{cosec}\theta - 1) + (\operatorname{cosec}\theta + 1)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta - 1}} = \dfrac{2\operatorname{cosec}\theta}{\sqrt{\cot^2\theta}} = \dfrac{2\operatorname{cosec}\theta}{\cot\theta}\)

(for an acute angle \(\cot\theta > 0\)). Then \(\dfrac{2\operatorname{cosec}\theta}{\cot\theta} = \dfrac{2/\sin\theta}{\cos\theta/\sin\theta} = \dfrac{2}{\cos\theta} = 2\sec\theta = \text{RHS}\).

rows.subtopic: Section Formula and Ratio of Division
rows.stem: If the mid-point of the line segment joining the points \(A(3, 4)\) and \(B(k, 6)\) is \(P(x, y)\) and \(x + y - 10 = 0\), then find the value of k.
rows.solution:
The mid-point of \(A(3, 4)\) and \(B(k, 6)\) is \(P\left(\dfrac{3 + k}{2}, \dfrac{4 + 6}{2}\right) = \left(\dfrac{3 + k}{2}, 5\right)\).

Since \(x + y - 10 = 0\): \(\dfrac{3 + k}{2} + 5 - 10 = 0\), so \(\dfrac{3 + k}{2} = 5\) and \(k = 7\).

rows.stem: The length of the hour hand of a clock is 10 cm. Find the area of the minor sector swept by the hour hand of the clock between 5 a.m. to 8 a.m. Also, find the area of the major sector.
rows.solution:
In one hour the hour hand turns \(\dfrac{360^\circ}{12} = 30^\circ\), so from 5 a.m. to 8 a.m. it sweeps \(3 \times 30^\circ = 90^\circ\).

Area of the minor sector \(= \dfrac{90}{360} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 10^2 = \dfrac{550}{7} \approx 78{\cdot}57\ \text{cm}^2\).

Area of the circle \(= \dfrac{22}{7} \times 10^2 = \dfrac{2200}{7}\ \text{cm}^2\).

Area of the major sector \(= \dfrac{2200}{7} - \dfrac{550}{7} = \dfrac{1650}{7} \approx 235{\cdot}71\ \text{cm}^2\).

rows.subtopic: Irrational Numbers and Proof by Contradiction
rows.stem: Prove that \(\sqrt{3}\) is an irrational number.
rows.solution:
Suppose, to the contrary, that \(\sqrt{3}\) is rational: \(\sqrt{3} = \dfrac{p}{q}\) with p and q co-prime integers and \(q \neq 0\).

Squaring, \(p^2 = 3q^2\). So \(p^2\) is divisible by 3, and since 3 is prime, p is divisible by 3. Write \(p = 3a\).

Then \(9a^2 = 3q^2\), so \(q^2 = 3a^2\) and q is divisible by 3 as well.

So 3 divides both p and q, contradicting that they are co-prime. Hence \(\sqrt{3}\) is irrational.

rows.stem: A sum of ₹ 2,000 is invested at 7% per annum simple interest. Calculate the interests at the end of \(1^{\text{st}}\), \(2^{\text{nd}}\) and \(3^{\text{rd}}\) year. Do these interests form an AP ? If so, find the interest at the end of the \(27^{\text{th}}\) year.
rows.solution:
Simple interest on ₹ 2,000 at 7% per annum for n years is \(\dfrac{2000 \times 7 \times n}{100} = 140n\).

End of year 1: ₹ 140; year 2: ₹ 280; year 3: ₹ 420.

These form an AP with first term 140 and common difference 140.

Interest at the end of the 27th year \(= a + 26d = 140 + 26 \times 140 = 27 \times 140 = ₹\ 3780\).

rows.stem: Two ships are sailing in the sea on either side of a lighthouse. The angles of depression to the two ships as observed from the top of the lighthouse are \(60^\circ\) and \(45^\circ\), respectively. If the distance between the ships is \(100\left(\dfrac{1 + \sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\) m, then find the height of the lighthouse.
rows.solution:
Let AB be the lighthouse (A the top, B the foot) and P, Q the two ships on either side. The angles of depression equal the angles of elevation at the ships: \(\angle APB = 60^\circ\) and \(\angle AQB = 45^\circ\).

In right triangle ABP: \(\tan 60^\circ = \dfrac{AB}{PB}\), so \(PB = \dfrac{AB}{\sqrt{3}}\).

In right triangle ABQ: \(\tan 45^\circ = \dfrac{AB}{BQ}\), so \(BQ = AB\).

So \(PQ = PB + BQ = AB\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} + 1\right) = AB\left(\dfrac{1 + \sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\).

Given \(PQ = 100\left(\dfrac{1 + \sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\), the height of the lighthouse is \(AB = 100\) m.

rows.stem: The angles of depression of the top and the bottom of an 8 m tall building from the top of another multistoried building are \(30^\circ\) and \(45^\circ\), respectively. Find the height of the multistoried building and the distance between the two buildings.
rows.solution:
Let CD be the multistoried building (D its top, C its foot) and AB the 8 m building (A its top, B its foot). Draw AE perpendicular to CD, so \(AE = BC\) and \(EC = AB = 8\) m.

The angle of depression of A from D is \(30^\circ\), so in right triangle DEA: \(\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{DE}{AE}\), giving \(AE = \sqrt{3}\,DE\).

The angle of depression of B from D is \(45^\circ\), so in right triangle DCB: \(\tan 45^\circ = \dfrac{DC}{BC}\), giving \(BC = DC\).

Since \(AE = BC\): \(\sqrt{3}\,DE = DC\), that is \(\sqrt{3}(DC - 8) = DC\).

So \(DC(\sqrt{3} - 1) = 8\sqrt{3}\) and \(DC = \dfrac{8\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3} - 1} = \dfrac{8\sqrt{3}(\sqrt{3} + 1)}{2} = 4\sqrt{3}(\sqrt{3} + 1) = (12 + 4\sqrt{3})\) m.

The multistoried building is \((12 + 4\sqrt{3})\) m tall, and the distance between the buildings is \(BC = DC = (12 + 4\sqrt{3})\) m.

rows.subtopic: Solving a Quadratic Equation by Factorisation
rows.stem: The sum of the areas of two squares is \(52\,\text{cm}^2\) and difference of their perimeters is 8 cm. Find the lengths of the sides of the two squares.
rows.solution:
Let the sides be x cm and y cm with \(x > y\).

Sum of areas: \(x^2 + y^2 = 52\). Difference of perimeters: \(4x - 4y = 8\), so \(x = y + 2\).

Substituting: \((y + 2)^2 + y^2 = 52\), so \(2y^2 + 4y - 48 = 0\), that is \(y^2 + 2y - 24 = 0\).

\((y + 6)(y - 4) = 0\), so \(y = 4\) (a length cannot be negative) and \(x = 6\).

The sides of the squares are 6 cm and 4 cm.

rows.subtopic: Solving a Quadratic Equation by Factorisation
rows.stem: The time taken by a person to travel an upward distance of 150 km was \(2\dfrac{1}{2}\) hours more than the time taken in the downward return journey. If he returned at a speed of 10 km/h more than the speed while going up, find the speeds in each direction.
rows.solution:
Let the upward speed be x km/h, so the downward speed is \((x + 10)\) km/h.

The upward journey takes \(2\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{5}{2}\) hours more: \(\dfrac{150}{x} - \dfrac{150}{x + 10} = \dfrac{5}{2}\).

\(\dfrac{1500}{x(x + 10)} = \dfrac{5}{2}\), so \(x(x + 10) = 600\), that is \(x^2 + 10x - 600 = 0\).

\((x + 30)(x - 20) = 0\), so \(x = 20\) (a speed cannot be negative).

The speed going up is 20 km/h and the speed coming down is 30 km/h.

rows.stem: Prove that a line drawn parallel to one side of a triangle to intersect the other two sides in distinct points divides the other two sides in the same ratio. Hence, in the figure given below, prove that \(\dfrac{AM}{MB} = \dfrac{AN}{ND}\) where \(LM \parallel CB\) and \(LN \parallel CD\).
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the quadrilateral ABCD with diagonal AC, L on AC, M on AB and N on AD is defined only by the drawing. Page idx 20.
rows.solution:
Theorem (Basic Proportionality Theorem). Given: in triangle ABC, a line parallel to BC meets AB at D and AC at E. To prove: \(\dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac{AE}{EC}\).

Construction: join BE and CD, and draw \(DM \perp AC\) and \(EN \perp AB\).

Proof: \(\dfrac{\text{ar}(ADE)}{\text{ar}(BDE)} = \dfrac{\frac{1}{2} AD \cdot EN}{\frac{1}{2} DB \cdot EN} = \dfrac{AD}{DB}\), and \(\dfrac{\text{ar}(ADE)}{\text{ar}(DEC)} = \dfrac{\frac{1}{2} AE \cdot DM}{\frac{1}{2} EC \cdot DM} = \dfrac{AE}{EC}\).

Triangles BDE and DEC are on the same base DE and between the same parallels DE and BC, so \(\text{ar}(BDE) = \text{ar}(DEC)\). Hence \(\dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac{AE}{EC}\).

Application: in triangle ABC, \(LM \parallel CB\), so by the theorem \(\dfrac{AM}{MB} = \dfrac{AL}{LC}\) ... (1)

In triangle ADC, \(LN \parallel CD\), so \(\dfrac{AN}{ND} = \dfrac{AL}{LC}\) ... (2)

From (1) and (2), \(\dfrac{AM}{MB} = \dfrac{AN}{ND}\).

rows.stem:

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.stem: Write down the pair of linear equations representing the given information.
rows.context:
A school is organizing a grand cultural event to show the talent of its students. To accommodate the guests, the school plans to rent chairs and tables from a local supplier. It finds that rent for each chair is ₹ 50 and for each table is ₹ 200. The school spends ₹ 30,000 for renting the chairs and tables. Also, the total number of items (chairs and tables) rented are 300.

If the school rents ‘x’ chairs and ‘y’ tables, answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: DECORATIVE - a photograph of a hall with chairs and tables; every number is in the passage. Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
x chairs and y tables are 300 items: \(x + y = 300\).

The rent is ₹ 30,000: \(50x + 200y = 30000\), that is \(x + 4y = 600\).

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.stem: Find the number of chairs and number of tables rented by the school.
rows.context:
A school is organizing a grand cultural event to show the talent of its students. To accommodate the guests, the school plans to rent chairs and tables from a local supplier. It finds that rent for each chair is ₹ 50 and for each table is ₹ 200. The school spends ₹ 30,000 for renting the chairs and tables. Also, the total number of items (chairs and tables) rented are 300.

If the school rents ‘x’ chairs and ‘y’ tables, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
Subtract \(x + y = 300\) from \(x + 4y = 600\): \(3y = 300\), so \(y = 100\) and \(x = 200\).

The school rented 200 chairs and 100 tables.

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.stem: If the school wants to spend a maximum of ₹ 27,000 on 300 items (tables and chairs), then find the number of chairs and tables it can rent.
rows.context:
A school is organizing a grand cultural event to show the talent of its students. To accommodate the guests, the school plans to rent chairs and tables from a local supplier. It finds that rent for each chair is ₹ 50 and for each table is ₹ 200. The school spends ₹ 30,000 for renting the chairs and tables. Also, the total number of items (chairs and tables) rented are 300.

If the school rents ‘x’ chairs and ‘y’ tables, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
Now \(x + y = 300\) and \(50x + 200y = 27000\), that is \(x + 4y = 540\).

Subtracting: \(3y = 240\), so \(y = 80\) and \(x = 220\).

The school can rent 220 chairs and 80 tables.

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.stem: What is maximum number of tables that can be rented in ₹ 30,000 if no chairs are rented ?
rows.context:
A school is organizing a grand cultural event to show the talent of its students. To accommodate the guests, the school plans to rent chairs and tables from a local supplier. It finds that rent for each chair is ₹ 50 and for each table is ₹ 200. The school spends ₹ 30,000 for renting the chairs and tables. Also, the total number of items (chairs and tables) rented are 300.

If the school rents ‘x’ chairs and ‘y’ tables, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
With no chairs, all ₹ 30,000 goes on tables at ₹ 200 each: \(\dfrac{30000}{200} = 150\).

At most 150 tables can be rented.

rows.subtopic: Probability from a Collection of Objects
rows.stem: What is the probability that Rahul draws a card with an even number ?
rows.context:
Rahul is a lucky charm for his cricket team. He has a jar of cards with numbers from 10 to 74. Before each match, he draws a card from the jar. If the card bears an even number, the team wins. If the number is even and divisible by 5, they win by a big margin. If the number is an odd number less than 30, they win by a small margin. And if the number is a prime number between 50 and 74, they lose.

Answer the following questions if Rahul draws a card today :
rows.figureNote: DECORATIVE - a photograph of a hand drawing a card from a jar; every number is in the passage. Page idx 24.
rows.solution:
The cards are numbered 10 to 74, so there are \(74 - 10 + 1 = 65\) equally likely cards.

The even numbers are \(10, 12, \ldots, 74\): \(\dfrac{74 - 10}{2} + 1 = 33\) cards.

\(P(\text{even}) = \dfrac{33}{65}\).

rows.subtopic: Probability from a Collection of Objects
rows.stem: What is the probability that Rahul draws a card with an odd number less than 30 ?
rows.context:
Rahul is a lucky charm for his cricket team. He has a jar of cards with numbers from 10 to 74. Before each match, he draws a card from the jar. If the card bears an even number, the team wins. If the number is even and divisible by 5, they win by a big margin. If the number is an odd number less than 30, they win by a small margin. And if the number is a prime number between 50 and 74, they lose.

Answer the following questions if Rahul draws a card today :
rows.solution:
The odd numbers less than 30 are \(11, 13, \ldots, 29\): 10 cards.

\(P(\text{odd and less than } 30) = \dfrac{10}{65} = \dfrac{2}{13}\).

rows.subtopic: Probability from a Collection of Objects
rows.stem: What is the probability that Rahul draws a card with a prime number between 50 and 74 ?
rows.context:
Rahul is a lucky charm for his cricket team. He has a jar of cards with numbers from 10 to 74. Before each match, he draws a card from the jar. If the card bears an even number, the team wins. If the number is even and divisible by 5, they win by a big margin. If the number is an odd number less than 30, they win by a small margin. And if the number is a prime number between 50 and 74, they lose.

Answer the following questions if Rahul draws a card today :
rows.solution:
The primes between 50 and 74 are 53, 59, 61, 67, 71 and 73: 6 cards.

\(P(\text{prime between 50 and 74}) = \dfrac{6}{65}\).

rows.subtopic: Probability from a Collection of Objects
rows.stem: What is the probability that Rahul draws a card with an even number divisible by 5 ?
rows.context:
Rahul is a lucky charm for his cricket team. He has a jar of cards with numbers from 10 to 74. Before each match, he draws a card from the jar. If the card bears an even number, the team wins. If the number is even and divisible by 5, they win by a big margin. If the number is an odd number less than 30, they win by a small margin. And if the number is a prime number between 50 and 74, they lose.

Answer the following questions if Rahul draws a card today :
rows.solution:
An even number divisible by 5 is a multiple of 10: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60 and 70, which is 7 cards.

\(P(\text{even and divisible by } 5) = \dfrac{7}{65}\).

rows.subtopic: Volume of a Combination of Solids
rows.stem: Find the volume of the bigger cylindrical part.
rows.context:
A skilled carpenter decided to craft a special rolling pin for the local baker. He carefully joined three cylindrical pieces of wood – two small ones on the ends and one larger in the centre to create a perfect tool. The baker loved the rolling pin, as it rolled out the smoothest dough for breads and pastries.

The length of the bigger cylindrical part is 12 cm and diameter is 7 cm and the length of each smaller cylindrical part is 5 cm and diameter is \(2{\cdot}1\) cm.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the dimensioned drawing of the rolling pin (two 5 cm by 2.1 cm end pieces on a 12 cm by 7 cm centre piece); every value is in the passage. The photograph above it is decorative. Page idx 26.
rows.solution:
The bigger part has radius \(\dfrac{7}{2}\) cm and length 12 cm.

Volume \(= \pi r^2 h = \dfrac{22}{7} \times \dfrac{7}{2} \times \dfrac{7}{2} \times 12 = 462\ \text{cm}^3\).

rows.subtopic: Surface Area of a Combination of Solids
rows.stem: Find the curved surface area of the bigger cylindrical part.
rows.context:
A skilled carpenter decided to craft a special rolling pin for the local baker. He carefully joined three cylindrical pieces of wood – two small ones on the ends and one larger in the centre to create a perfect tool. The baker loved the rolling pin, as it rolled out the smoothest dough for breads and pastries.

The length of the bigger cylindrical part is 12 cm and diameter is 7 cm and the length of each smaller cylindrical part is 5 cm and diameter is \(2{\cdot}1\) cm.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the dimensioned drawing of the rolling pin; every value is in the passage. Page idx 26.
rows.solution: Curved surface area \(= 2\pi r h = 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times \dfrac{7}{2} \times 12 = 264\ \text{cm}^2\).

rows.subtopic: Volume of a Combination of Solids
rows.stem: Find the ratio of the volume of the bigger cylindrical part to the total volume of the two smaller (identical) cylindrical parts.
rows.context:
A skilled carpenter decided to craft a special rolling pin for the local baker. He carefully joined three cylindrical pieces of wood – two small ones on the ends and one larger in the centre to create a perfect tool. The baker loved the rolling pin, as it rolled out the smoothest dough for breads and pastries.

The length of the bigger cylindrical part is 12 cm and diameter is 7 cm and the length of each smaller cylindrical part is 5 cm and diameter is \(2{\cdot}1\) cm.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the dimensioned drawing of the rolling pin; every value is in the passage. Page idx 26.
rows.solution:
Each smaller part has radius \(\dfrac{2{\cdot}1}{2} = 1{\cdot}05\) cm and length 5 cm.

Total volume of the two \(= 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 1{\cdot}05 \times 1{\cdot}05 \times 5 = 34{\cdot}65\ \text{cm}^3\).

Ratio \(= \dfrac{462}{34{\cdot}65} = \dfrac{3080}{231} = \dfrac{40}{3}\).

The ratio of the volume of the bigger part to the total volume of the two smaller parts is \(40 : 3\) (equivalently \(3080 : 231\)).

rows.subtopic: Surface Area of a Combination of Solids
rows.stem: Find the sum of the curved surface areas of the two identical smaller cylindrical parts.
rows.context:
A skilled carpenter decided to craft a special rolling pin for the local baker. He carefully joined three cylindrical pieces of wood – two small ones on the ends and one larger in the centre to create a perfect tool. The baker loved the rolling pin, as it rolled out the smoothest dough for breads and pastries.

The length of the bigger cylindrical part is 12 cm and diameter is 7 cm and the length of each smaller cylindrical part is 5 cm and diameter is \(2{\cdot}1\) cm.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the dimensioned drawing of the rolling pin; every value is in the passage. Page idx 26.
rows.solution: Sum of the curved surface areas of the two smaller parts \(= 2 \times 2\pi r h = 2 \times 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 1{\cdot}05 \times 5 = 66\ \text{cm}^2\).
